title: Runtime profiling: KV-cache, quantization, TRT-LLM vs vLLM (deep dive)
summary: Deep technical session focusing on GPU runtime profiling across TRT-LLM and vLLM stacks. Key topics: kernel selection heuristics, CUDA graph capture pitfalls with dynamic seq lengths, eviction-aware batching and KV-cache design, quantization tradeoffs for 4-bit/8-bit, and on-prem/VPC constraints for benchmarking. Action items: share raw traces, run standardized trtexec and vLLM traces, schedule follow-up benchmark window.
next_steps: Maya to upload TRT and vLLM profiling traces + Nsight captures (link) by 2025-10-06
AtlaSys to run provided trtexec script on their on-prem A100 cluster and share logs by 2025-10-09
Schedule 1-hour follow-up for TSV analysis and canary config on 2025-10-14
action_items: Maya Patel - Send trtexec + vllm run scripts, and a short 'how to capture CUDA graphs' note - due 2025-10-06
Priya Nair - Prepare a small write-up comparing fused attention kernels we saw vs fallback cuBLAS kernels (include perf numbers) - due 2025-10-08
Samir Gupta - Run AtlaSys A100 benchmark with 2 sequence lengths (128/2048) using provided scripts and upload traces - due 2025-10-09
Diego Morales - Share infra constraints (VPC subnet, KMS access, noisy neighbor windows) so Redwood can simulate - due 2025-10-07
transcript:
[Meeting header] 2025-10-02 09:23 UTC | Duration: ~74 minutes | Attendees: Maya (Redwood), Priya (Redwood SE), Liam (Infra), Samir (AtlaSys CTO), Rachel (ML Lead), Diego (SRE)

00:00 Maya (AE): hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. quick check — audio ok?
00:06 Samir (CTO): yeah sounds good, uh, thanks. excited to dig in.
00:12 Priya (SE): cool, I'll share my screen in a sec. agenda — kernel selection, cudagraphs capture issues, kv cache behavior under eviction, and quantization tradeoffs across TRT-LLM and vLLM. plus an on-prem runbook for benchmarking.
00:25 Rachel (ML): fine by us. for context, we're running mostly Mistral/LLama 2 variants right now and have an internal A100 on-prem cluster behind a VPC.
00:38 Liam (Infra): and we have some tenant isolation via subnet + firewall rules; we can open ephemeral SSH for profiling.
00:44 Maya: perfect. quick note — we put links in the calendar: trtexec script, a tiny vllm run script, and the profiling checklist.

03:05 Priya: ok first slide — kernel selection. the runtime tries to pick fused kernels for attention when the shape and dtype match the compiled kernels. if shapes vary — for example when seq-len dynamic range is wide — we often fall back to cuBLAS kernels which are slower. you can see in the trace where the op name switches to matmul or gemm fallback.
03:38 Rachel: is that the thing that causes latency spikes during prefix expansion? we saw some 100ms spikes when chat histories get long.
03:47 Priya: yes, exactly. prefix/KV cache growth changes the per-step shape and sometimes the compiled graph doesn't match so it ejects, or the CUDA graph capture fails to include the dynamic path.
04:05 Samir: hmm, and is that more common on TRT-LLM or vLLM?
04:12 Priya: good question. TRT-LLM tends to be more brittle with CUDA graphs if you have varying seq len, because it loves fully static shapes for the best fused kernels. vLLM's dynamic kernel selection is more flexible, so you might see steadier latency but at slightly higher peak throughput in some configs. also, vLLM is better at batching dynamic shapes at runtime.

07:00 Liam: we noticed memory fragmentation on the A100 after long runs; eventually performance degenerated. is that a known issue?
07:10 Priya: yeah fragmentation and allocator churn — especially with small KV cache allocations — can hurt long-lived servers. our runtime uses a slab allocator and tries to reuse KV buffers, but if your access patterns evict frequently you'll see churn. eviction-aware batching helps: keep a small hot-KV window pinned to faster memory and let cold entries be stored in quantized buffers.
07:45 Diego (SRE): by "quantized buffers" do you mean we store cold keys in 4-bit? that's kind of scary for accuracy.
07:51 Priya: we mean low-precision caches for cold prefixes — typically we only quantize KV that aren't used in the next N steps. we saw negligible regen quality falloff for many workloads with GPTQ-style 4-bit for keys+values, but you should validate with your prompts.

10:30 Maya: jumping to CUDA graphs — common pitfall is capturing a graph on a warmup input then replaying on longer sequences. CUDA graph capture bakes shapes and launch parameters; if you run a longer seq after capture, the graph may fail or trigger a fallback path causing a big latency spike.
10:55 Samir: we've been capturing graphs in CI to reduce the runtime jitter. any tips to get stable captures?
11:03 Priya: capture multiple graphs for common hotspots: short (<=128), medium (512), long (2048). then use policy routing: pick graph by likely bucket. also capture different batch-sizes if you vary workloads. avoid capturing on sequences that include new tokens appended dynamically — capture on representative steady-state sampling.

14:20 Rachel: comparing TRT-LLM vs vLLM — what's the rough rule of thumb for us if we care about 95th percentile latency vs throughput/cost?
14:30 Priya: TRT-LLM typically wins on peak throughput and raw TFlops when shapes are static and you can compile a fully fused kernel graph. vLLM wins for dynamic latency SLOs and smaller tail variance because of its dynamic dispatcher and more tolerant kernel fallbacks. so if you can afford model pinning and static inputs, TRT-LLM for cost-effiency; if chat-like dynamic inputs with varying history, vLLM reduces tail latency surprises.

18:00 Diego: I want to call out CUDA graph warmups cause trouble with our VPC setup — sometimes the first compiled graph needs additional temp memory and our networked NVMe is slow so it spills. any suggestions?
18:15 Priya: pre-warm on the same host where the model will run; avoid remote prewarm over network. if you must use a shared disk, increase tmpfs or ensure local SSD for transient allocations. also monitor /proc/driver/nvidia/gpus and dmesg for any OOMs.

21:40 Maya: quantization — we heard you use GPTQ in some cases. what about int8 or fused 8-bit kernels in TRT-LLM?
21:50 Priya: TRT-LLM has some int8 paths but they require calibration and are more brittle for attention. 4-bit GPTQ often gives better model-size wins with less perf regression for LLMs but you need a per-model calibrator. our suggestion: try 4-bit quant for KV caches and 8-bit for weights only if you run extensive evals. by the way, mixed-precision FP16 + per-op fallback sometimes gives the best stability/perf balance.

25:10 Samir: any real numbers? we ran a 1k token generation test: TRT-LLM (static seq) got 24 tokens/s at batch 8, vLLM got 18 tokens/s but 95th latency was much lower.
25:25 Priya: those numbers match our internal quick runs. important to compare apples-to-apples: same batch, same dtype, same model artifact (no different tokenizer or fused ops disabled). we attached a small spreadsheet in the calendar with sample numbers.

29:00 Rachel: let's talk about eviction-aware batching. we saw throughput drop when many sessions had long tails.
29:10 Priya: eviction-aware batching groups requests by hot-KV affinity. so requests that can reuse same cached K/V are batched together; cold sessions are either served from quantized cold-store or routed to a cheaper lane. it's similar to sharding by working-set. that reduces duplication of KV loads and lowers per-token memory pressure.
29:45 Diego: what about correctness — if keys are quantized and we rehydrate frequently, does that add latency?
29:55 Priya: rehydration has a cost; typically you amortize by doing it in background and only rehydrate when a session becomes hot. for our customers we saw rehydrate cost < 5% of token latency when background threads and pinned memory were used.

33:30 Liam: from infra perspective, we worry about benchmarking parity between our VPC and Redwood hosted numbers. any tips for on-prem fair runs?
33:40 Priya: yes — 1) pin CPU governors to performance, 2) disable power c-states for the experiment, 3) isolate the GPU via nvidia-smi mig or set persistence mode, 4) ensure same CUDA/CUDNN/TensorRT versions as Redwood's suggested stack, 5) capture Nsight+CUDA profiler traces.
34:05 Maya: we also suggest a two-window benchmark: one micro-benchmark (trtexec/vllm speed only) and one application-level run that includes network, auth, and prefix logic. the micro-benchmarks should match within ~5-10% if stack versions and drivers are aligned.

38:00 Samir: one weird failure we saw — cudagraph capture throws 'invalid argument' when batch size changes mid-capture. is that expected?
38:10 Priya: yes that's expected. capture is strict. the only workaround is capturing multiple graphs or using a replay engine that supports dynamic parameters (we have an experimental shim that does this, we'll share).

41:30 Rachel: should we try the TRT-LLM static compile path for our high-throughput batch inference while using vLLM for chat? hybrid approach?
41:38 Priya: that's exactly one common pattern. route requests by policy: high-throughput offline jobs -> TRT-LLM pinned model variant; interactive chat -> vLLM with eviction-aware batching and smaller batch sizes. fallback policies if capacity low.

45:55 Maya: note on model versions — if you compile a TRT-LLM engine against a model with fused ops, any small tokenizer change can invalidate the compiled engine. ensure model artifact immutability in the pipeline.
46:12 Samir: good to know. we've seen failed rollouts due to that.

49:00 Diego: any monitoring hooks we should enable to see when kernel fallbacks are occurring in prod?
49:10 Priya: yes instrument kernel names in traces — the runtime already records the kernel type (fused vs fallback) and we emit metrics for fallback-count, graph-miss-rate, and eviction-rate. set alerts for graph-miss-rate > 2% or fallback-count spikes.

52:30 Rachel: security angle — on-prem VPC and KMS: as we run profiling, any keys or traces that may leave our cluster?
52:40 Maya: no — for the benchmark runs we recommend sharing only sanitized traces (no raw prompt text). you can redact PII from traces. for KMS access we can provide a read-only service account and a temporary key if needed. also for private deployments Redwood can run with customer-managed KMS/HSM.

56:00 Priya: quick demo — I'm showing two Nsight flamegraphs: left is TRT-LLM with a fused attention kernel spike at 35ms, right is vLLM where you see many smaller kernels but lower tail. note the cudaGraph capture sections highlighted — the TRT capture removed 10% overhead but when a graph-miss occurs you get a 3x spike.
56:45 Samir: can you share these captures? the visualizations are helpful.
56:50 Priya: yes I'll share the Nsight project and the raw .ncu and .nsys files.

60:00 Maya: recap and decisions — AtlaSys will try two experiments: 1) Run TRT-LLM compile path on a static pinned model for batch jobs and share traces. 2) Run vLLM baseline for chat sessions enabling eviction-aware batching and quantized cold-KV. Redwood will provide scripts and a small write-up.
60:30 Samir: yep we'll run both. question on timelines — can we get Redwood's initial artifact by next Monday?
60:38 Maya: yes, sending trtexec and vllm scripts + quick 'how-to' by 2025-10-06.

66:15 Rachel: one last practical note — our tokenization pipeline does some on-the-fly pretokenization which changes sequence shapes subtly. should we normalize that for the benchmarks?
66:25 Priya: yes normalize. run with identical tokenizer config and batch grouping. small differences in input lengths can change kernel selection.

72:00 Maya: thanks everyone. I'll follow up with the spreadsheet and a calendar invite for the follow-up.
72:08 Samir: thanks all, very actionable.
72:15 Diego: thanks. bye.
